description: Software engineer and coffee grower on Saturdays
summary:
Tempo helps smallholder farmers and extension agents in Central America's Dry Corridor decide what to plant in the postrera, the second planting season (September–November), after the midsummer dry spell known as the canícula.

A user taps their plot on a map. Tempo pulls 25 years (2001–2025) of NASA GPM IMERG satellite rainfall, NASA POWER weather, SRTM terrain and SoilGrids soil data for that exact point, runs a simplified crop water balance based on FAO-56, and compares three common options: relay bean after maize, sorghum (maicillo) with bean, and second-season maize.

It recommends the option with the best worst case across explicit uncertainty scenarios (IMERG vs. POWER rainfall, a 150 mm late-rain rule for beans, and soil water capacity) and labels its confidence as high, medium or low, explaining what keeps it from being higher.

Near Nacaome, Honduras, the 2026 canícula lasted 18 days and July–August brought 43 mm of rain against a 331 mm normal. Tempo turns NASA's satellite record into an honest, plot-level decision aid. It does not estimate yields and is not yet field-validated.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Tempo is a map-based web app. The user taps a point in the Dry Corridor (El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua) or types coordinates. Tempo downloads that point's data, runs the model and shows which of three postrera planting options best withstands its worst plausible scenario, with a confidence level (high, medium, low) and a plain-language reason why confidence is not higher.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data: daily rainfall from NASA GPM IMERG V07 (half-hourly, aggregated to local days, 2001–2025) via Google Earth Engine; temperature, humidity, radiation and backup rainfall from the NASA POWER Daily API; elevation and slope from SRTM GL1 30 m; soil texture and carbon (0–30 cm) from ISRIC SoilGrids v2.

2. Model: a simplified WRSI-style water balance (FAO-56 crop coefficients, Hargreaves ET0) per crop and season.

3. Decision: each option is scored under explicit scenarios (IMERG vs. POWER rainfall, with and without the 150 mm bean rule, soil water capacity of 60/90/130 mm). Tempo picks the best worst case (maximin) and assigns confidence from the margins and stability across scenarios.

4. Validation: leave-one-out hindcast 2001–2025 with no circularity (the target year never enters validation). External checks: the model places 31 of 54 documented drought cases (2001, 2009, 2014, 2015, 2018, 2019; cited from FAO, FEWS NET, WFP, ReliefWeb) among its worst years, against about 32% by chance. Against a NOAA GHCN-Daily rain gauge (Tegucigalpa), IMERG overestimates July–August rain by 77% but tracks year-to-year changes well (Spearman r = 0.85). Comparison with FAOSTAT national yields is weak except for maize in El Salvador.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Farmers in the Dry Corridor lose harvests when the canícula runs long. Regional systems such as FEWS NET GeoWRSI and FAO ASIS show where stress occurs. Tempo answers a different, plot-level question: which planting option holds up best in a season like this one, and how sure are we? It is designed for extension agents and cooperatives working with smallholders.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- Uncertainty is shown as explicit scenarios, not hidden: the app explains why it is not more confident.

- Honesty by design: none of the 9 analyzed points reaches high confidence (6 low, 3 medium), and the app says so.

- Serverless demo mode: 9 real precomputed analyses that run as a static site, so they work on low connectivity.

- Spanish and English interface, mobile-friendly, light and dark mode.

TOOLS

Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, requests), Google Earth Engine Python API, NASA POWER API, SoilGrids REST API, a Python HTTP server, vanilla JavaScript, HTML and CSS, Leaflet 1.9.4, OpenStreetMap and Esri World Imagery tiles, pytest and Playwright for tests.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

Satellite rainfall bias in mountain valleys, assumptions that are not validated yet (the 150 mm bean rule, FAO-56 crop parameters), the lack of local yield data, avoiding circular validation, and communicating confidence to non-technical users.

LIMITS AND NEXT STEPS

Tempo is not field-validated and does not estimate yields or income. Next steps: validate crop parameters and the bean rule with local agronomists (CENTA), compare with more local rain stations, and test against municipal yields.

USE OF AI

AI assistants (Claude, Devin) helped write and debug code and tests, audit the model, and draft the presentation text. All results were checked against automated tests and the source data. No AI-generated images, audio or video are used.
